1.3a — Your First Script: Variables & Update

Today you write C# that runs inside your game. Not by copying lines someone else wrote, but by reading Unity's core engine documentation, analyzing an analogous diagnostic script, and engineering your own custom logger from scratch.

Read the Docs ~15 min

Every script in Unity that attaches to a GameObject inherits from MonoBehaviour. This base class connects your code to the engine's game loop and provides key lifecycle methods:

Engine APISignature / TypeDescription & Behavior
Start() void Start() Lifecycle hook. Called automatically by Unity exactly once before the first frame of gameplay. Used for initialization and caching references.
Update() void Update() Lifecycle hook. Called automatically every single frame. At 60 FPS, this runs 60 times per second. Used for polling input, updating timers, and continuous logic.
Debug.Log() void Debug.Log(object message) Prints a string or value directly to the Unity Console window. Essential developer feedback for seeing what your code is doing.
Time.time float (read-only) The total elapsed time in seconds since the game entered Play mode. Constantly increases while the game runs.
[SerializeField] Attribute prefix: [SerializeField] private float speed; Instructs Unity to serialize the private field and display it as an editable control in the Inspector window without exposing it to other classes.

Socratic: Lifecycle and Timing

  1. If your computer runs the game at 120 FPS, how many times will Update() execute in a single second? What if it runs on a battery-saving laptop at 30 FPS?
  2. If you write Debug.Log("hello") directly inside Update() without an interval check, what happens to your Unity Console in 5 seconds?
  3. Why does software engineering encourage [SerializeField] private rather than making every field public? (Hint: Who should be allowed to change a component's internal variables?)
Read Function-Level Examples ~15 min

Never look for an entire script to copy. In real software engineering, you read how individual functions and language features work in isolation, then assemble them into your own architecture. Look at these isolated snippets from completely different systems:

Example 1 — Exposing an Inspector Knob on a Weather Station:

// Exposes an editable tuning knob in the Inspector while keeping the variable private
[SerializeField] private float windSamplingRate = 2.5f;

Example 2 — Printing Diagnostic Output from a Submarine:

// Sends developer feedback to the Unity Console, combining strings with variables
Debug.Log("Submarine sonar ping sent at depth: " + currentDepth + "m");

Example 3 — Rate-Limiting Execution with Engine Time on a Lighthouse:

// Gates an action so it only runs once an interval has elapsed, instead of every frame
if (Time.time >= nextFlashTimestamp)
{
    Debug.Log("Lighthouse beacon flashed at: " + Time.time);
    nextFlashTimestamp = Time.time + flashInterval; // Schedule next flash in the future
}

Predict Before Building

  1. In the lighthouse snippet, why does nextFlashTimestamp = Time.time + flashInterval; prevent the message from printing 60 times a second?
  2. If flashInterval is 3.0f and the game started 5 seconds ago, when will the next pulse be allowed to fire?
Build Lab: Your Turn ~25 min

Your Engineering Mission: Build PlayerLogger.cs. You will create your own custom diagnostic script from scratch and attach it to the Player GameObject.

Architectural Specification for PlayerLogger.cs:
  1. File & Class Name: In Assets/Scripts/, create a new C# script named PlayerLogger.cs. The class name inside the file must match the filename exactly.
  2. Inspector Knob: Declare a serialized private float field named reportDelay with a default value of 1.0f.
  3. Timestamp Memory: Declare a private float field named nextReportTime initialized to 0f.
  4. Timed Execution in Update: In Update(), write an if statement that checks whether the current Time.time is greater than or equal to nextReportTime.
  5. Action & Advancement: Inside the if branch, log a message showing the current time (e.g. "Player active at: " + Time.time), then advance nextReportTime by adding reportDelay to Time.time.
  6. Attach to Player: In the Unity Editor, select the Player in the Hierarchy and attach your PlayerLogger component.

Press Play in Unity and open the Console window (Window → General → Console). Verify that your logger prints once per second without spamming hundreds of lines per second!

Bug Hunt: Break the Logger on Purpose

Introduce each issue temporarily to understand the engine error states, then fix it:

  1. Rename the class to playerLogger (lowercase p) in the code while leaving the file named PlayerLogger.cs. What error appears in Unity when you press Play?
  2. Attach the script to the Turret instead of the Player. Does it still run? What does this prove about how components relate to GameObjects?
  3. Comment out the line that advances nextReportTime. What happens to the Console output within 2 seconds?
Tinker ~10 min

Tinker: Extending the Logger

  1. While the game is running, select the Player and change reportDelay to 0.25 in the Inspector. What happens to the print rate? When you stop the game, what value does reportDelay revert to?
  2. Modify your log statement to output the object's position: transform.position. What 3-dimensional data structure does it print?
  3. Add a second serialized field: [SerializeField] private int maxReports = 5;. How would you prevent the logger from running once it has logged 5 times?

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Create a new C# script and attach it to a GameObject as a component
  • Explain what runs when: Start() once vs Update() every frame
  • Write a [SerializeField] private field and explain how it differs from a public field
  • Explain the critical rule: C# class name must match filename 1:1
  • Implement interval-based execution with Time.time instead of spamming every frame
